\]

\[
a=\inf\{u\in\mathbb R:[u,x]\subseteq O\},\qquad b=\sup\{v\in\mathbb R:[x,v]\subseteq O\}.
\]
Because $O$ is open and contains $x$, we have $a<x<b$. If $a<z<b$, choose $u<z$ with $[u,x]\subseteq O$ and $v>z$ with $[x,v]\subseteq O$. Then $z\in O$, and $[\min(x,z),\max(x,z)]\subseteq O$, so $z\in C_x$. Conversely, if $z\in C_x$ and $z<x$, then $z$ belongs to the first defining set, so $z>a$; if $z>x$, then $z<b$. Hence $C_x=(a,b)$.

Therefore $O$ is a disjoint union of open intervals. Each nonempty open interval contains a rational number, and disjoint intervals contain distinct rationals. Since $\mathbb Q$ is countable, there are at most countably many such intervals.\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Let $O$ be open in $\mathbb R$. For $x,y\in O$, write $x\sim y$ when the entire closed interval between them lies in $O$:
\[
x\sim y\iff [\min(x,y),\max(x,y)]\subseteq O.
\]
Reflexivity and symmetry are clear. For transitivity, suppose $x\sim y$ and $y\sim z$. Every point between $x$ and $z$ lies either between $x$ and $y$ or between $y$ and $z$, so
\[
[\min(x,z),\max(x,z)]\subseteq [\min(x,y),\max(x,y)]\cup[\min(y,z),\max(y,z)]\subseteq O.
\]
Thus $\sim$ is an equivalence relation.

For $x\in O$, let $C_x$ denote its equivalence class. Set
\[
a=\inf A,\quad A=\{u\in\mathbb R:[u,x]\subseteq O\},
\qquad
b=\sup B,\quad B=\{v\in\mathbb R:[x,v]\subseteq O\}.
\]
The openness of $O$ at $x$ implies $A$ contains points less than $x$ and $B$ contains points greater than $x$, so $a<x<b$. If $a<z<b$, choose $u\in A$ with $u<z$ and $v\in B$ with $v>z$. Then $z\in [u,x]\cup[x,v]\subseteq O$, and the interval between $x$ and $z$ is contained in $O$; hence $z\in C_x$. Conversely, if $z\in C_x$ and $z<x$, then $z\in A$, so $z\ge a$, and in fact $z>a$ because $z\in O$ and $O$ is open. Similarly, if $z>x$, then $z<b$. Therefore $C_x=(a,b)$.

The equivalence classes are pairwise disjoint and cover $O$, so $O$ is a disjoint union of open intervals. Assign to each interval a rational number it contains. Disjoint intervals receive distinct rationals, giving an injection into $\mathbb Q$. Hence the collection is at most countable.\end{proof}

\[
x\sim y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad [\min(x,y),\max(x,y)]\subseteq O.
\]

Fix $x\in O$ and define
\[
A_x=\{u\in\mathbb R:u\le x\text{ and }[u,x]\subseteq O\},
\quad
B_x=\{v\in\mathbb R:v\ge x\text{ and }[x,v]\subseteq O\}.
\]
Let $a=\inf A_x$ and $b=\sup B_x$. Since $O$ is open and contains $x$, $a<x<b$. If $a<z<b$, there are $u\in A_x$ and $v\in B_x$ with $u<z<v$, so $z\in O$ and the interval between $x$ and $z$ is contained in $O. Hence $z\sim x$. Conversely, if $z\sim x$ and $z<x$, then $z\in A_x$, and because $z\in O$ while $O$ is open, $z>a$; similarly, if $z>x$, then $z<b$. Therefore the equivalence class of $x$ is exactly $(a,b)$.

Consequently, $O$ is the union of its pairwise disjoint equivalence classes, each of which is an open interval. Every nonempty open interval contains a rational number. Choosing one rational in each interval gives an injection from the intervals into $\mathbb Q$, so there are at most countably many.\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Let $O$ be an open subset of $\mathbb R$. For $x,y\in O$, define
\[
x\sim y\iff [\min(x,y),\max(x,y)]\subseteq O.
\]
The relation is reflexive and symmetric. If $x\sim y$ and $y\sim z$, then, after possibly reversing the order of the three points, the interval between the extreme points is the union of two subintervals, one between $x,y$ and one between $y,z$. Hence it is contained in $O$, proving transitivity.

Fix $x\in O$ and let
\[
A=\{u\le x:[u,x]\subseteq O\},\qquad B=\{v\ge x:[x,v]\subseteq O\},
\]
with $a=\inf A$ and $b=\sup B$. Since $O$ is open at $x$, there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subseteq O$, so $a<x<b$.

We claim that the equivalence class of $x$ is $(a,b)$. If $a<z<b$, choose $u\in A$ and $v\in B$ such that $u<z<v$. If $z\le x$, then $[z,x]\subseteq[u,x]\subseteq O$; if $z\ge x$, then $[x,z]\subseteq[x,v]\subseteq O$. Thus $z\sim x$. Conversely, suppose $z\sim x$. If $z<x$, then $z\in A$. Since $z\in O$ and $O$ is open, some point smaller than $z$ also belongs to $A$, so $z>a$. If $z>x$, the analogous argument gives $z<b$. Therefore the class is $(a,b)$.

The equivalence classes partition $O$, and each class is an open interval. To each class assign a rational number it contains. Distinct classes are disjoint, so these rationals are distinct. This injects the set of classes into the countable set $\mathbb Q$. Thus $O$ is the union of an at most countable collection of pairwise disjoint segments (indeed, open intervals).\end{proof}
